# Summary



# Data

The panel covers 10 provinces and 54 quarters, from 2012Q3 to 2025Q4 (540 province-quarters). The CMHC data used here was published in March 2026.

*[Sources: CMHC delinquency, Labour Force Survey unemployment, Bank of Canada policy rate.]*

# Methods

## Why a panel with fixed effects

Provinces differ permanently in ways I cannot observe or measure well, such as housing market structure, lending practices and demographics. Province fixed effects remove these constant differences, so the model compares each province with itself over time: what happens to delinquency in a province when its unemployment changes. This removes omitted variables that are constant within a province, but not those that change over time, which I discuss in the next section. Quarter-of-year effects absorb seasonality. I do not include a full set of date effects, because they would absorb the national policy rate, which only varies over time.

## Omitted variable bias

A fixed effects model adds a dummy variable for each province. These dummies control for any characteristic, observed or not, that is constant within a province over time. They do not control for factors that change over time within a province and move with unemployment, such as local income or house prices. If such factors exist, the unemployment coefficient is biased, and I cannot say in which direction. It as an association, not as a causal effect. The robustness checks show how much of the association is shared across places: in the metropolitan-area models, the coefficient falls from 0.154 to 0.093 when I remove shocks common to all areas in a quarter, and to 0.034 when I compare areas within the same province and quarter. Part of the association reflects common shocks.

## COVID

The COVID period was atypical: payment deferrals and income support likely pushed delinquency down while unemployment spiked, which broke the usual relationship between the two. I set these quarters apart with an indicator for 2020Q2 to 2021Q4. In the main model, the indicator is about -0.50, meaning delinquency was roughly 40% lower in those quarters than unemployment and the policy rate would predict. I also estimate the model without those quarters, and the unemployment coefficient rises from 0.171 to 0.228.


## Inference

*[Errors clustered by province, only 10 clusters, why I repeat the models with 33 metropolitan areas.]*

## Out-of-sample validation

The baseline model is a panel regression with province and quarter-of-year fixed effects, used to measure the association between unemployment, the policy rate and delinquency. To see whether a more flexible model predicts better, I also fit random forests (500 trees, no tuning), which do not assume a functional form and can capture nonlinear effects. 

There is a comparison of all models on quarters they were not fitted on. For each of the 16 test quarters (2022Q1 to 2025Q4), I refit every model on all earlier data and predict one quarter ahead, which gives 160 predictions per model. The reference is a model that only uses last quarter’s delinquency, and I measure error as RMSE in log points. To test whether differences between models are real,  a Diebold-Mariano is performed to test on the average error per quarter. As there are only 16 test quarters the test has low power.

# Results




## Association with unemployment and the policy rate

*[Text.]*

```{r}
#| label: fe-table
fe_file <- c("fixed_effects_models.csv", "baseline_models.csv")
fe_file <- fe_file[file.exists(out(fe_file))][1]
rd(fe_file) |>
  mutate(term = recode(term, !!!term_labels),
         cell = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", estimate, std.error)) |>
  select(term, model, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = cell) |>
  kable(caption = "Provincial fixed-effects models. Coefficient (standard error).")
```

![](`r fig("rate_lag_profile.png")`)

## Robustness with 33 metropolitan areas

*[Text.]*

```{r}
#| label: cma-table
rd("cma_models.csv") |>
  mutate(term = recode(term, !!!term_labels),
         cell = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", estimate, std.error)) |>
  select(term, model, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = cell) |>
  kable(caption = "Metropolitan-area models. Coefficient (standard error).")
```

## Heterogeneity by province

Unemployment is positive in all provinces. In the provincial panel it ranges from 0.09 (Alberta) to 0.30 (Prince Edward Island), and in the metropolitan-area panel from 0.09 (Alberta) to 0.23 (British Columbia). British Columbia in the provincial panel has a lower bound just below zero (-0.001). Each estimate uses about 50 quarters of a highly persistent series, and metropolitan areas within a province are not independent. I therefore treat the intervals as indicative and do not rank provinces.

![](`r fig("heterogeneity.png")`)

## Prediction

*[Text.]*

```{r}
#| label: validation-table
rd("validation_scores_all.csv") |>
  mutate(model = recode(model, !!!model_labels)) |>
  select(Model = model, MSE = mse, RMSE = rmse, MAE = mae) |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Out-of-sample error, 16 test quarters. Log points.")
```

*[Text.]*

